lead: A text file is a sequence of characters stored on disk. Python does not edit the disk directly; it asks open() for a file object, and that object holds a pointer. The pointer marks the next character to read or write. This matters because marks, bills and log files live as text, and a program must move from writing a line to reading it back. The same object serves read(), readline(), write(), tell() and seek().
prereq: You need: 5.1 for FileNotFoundError, and Unit 3 strings for strip() and split().

blocks.text: open(path, mode) returns a file object. path is a string such as 'marks.txt'. mode is a short string that decides what the program may do. The file object holds a pointer: the position of the next character to read or write. At open in 'r' or 'w', the pointer is at 0. In 'a', it is at the end of the file.

items: 'r': read only. The file must exist; otherwise open() raises FileNotFoundError.
'w': write only. It erases an existing file at once, before the first write.
'a': append. Writes go to the end; existing text stays.
'r+': read and write. It does not erase the file.

blocks.text: Add 'b' for binary bytes, for example 'rb'; text work uses no 'b'. Use encoding='utf-8' once when text has characters outside plain ASCII. tell() returns the current pointer position as an opaque number. For plain ASCII text it equals the character count; with non-ASCII text under UTF-8 it is a byte offset and can be larger. seek(0) moves the pointer to the start. In text mode, any other seek() call must use a value that tell() returned earlier. Opening a file does not load the whole file into memory.

f.write(s) writes string s and returns the number of characters written. It adds no newline; put '\n' in the string yourself. f.writelines(list) writes each string in the list, again with no newline added. A file stores text, not numbers. To write 78, use str(78); f.write(78) raises TypeError.

f.read() returns all remaining text as one string. f.read(n) returns the next n characters. f.readline() returns the next line, including its '\n', or '' at end of file. f.readlines() returns a list of the remaining lines. for line in f: reads one line per turn without loading the whole file.

Each read moves the pointer forward by the characters consumed. To read a number back, take the line, use strip() to remove '\n' and spaces, then int() or float(). For two fields, parts = line.split() gives strings; int(parts[1]) gives the mark. The file does not remember that 78 was a number.

close() flushes buffered data to disk and releases the operating-system handle. Data may sit in memory until close() or flush(). The with statement closes for you even if an exception occurs: with open('marks.txt', 'r') as f: then an indented block. Use with for normal work. If open() fails, with never enters; catch FileNotFoundError with try/except from 5.1. A closed file cannot be read or written; Python raises ValueError. seek(0) returns to the start; a second read() after read() returns only the remaining text.

figure.caption: marks.txt starts with the 8 characters 'Anil 78\n'. open() creates a file object; in 'r' or 'w' the pointer is at 0, and in 'a' it is at the end. readline() returns the first line and moves the pointer to 8; close() flushes buffered text to disk. The value 8 from tell() is a character count only because this text is ASCII.

spec.aria: open() creates a file object; in modes r and w the pointer starts at 0, and in mode a it starts at the end. marks.txt starts with 'Anil 78\n'. readline() returns that first line and pushes the pointer to position 8, a dashed edge back to readline shows the next call, and close() writes the buffered data to disk. tell() reports 8 because this text is ASCII.

examples.question: Write the two lines Anil 78 and Bina 91 into marks.txt, close it, append Chetan 65, then read the first line and report the pointer.
steps: Use open('marks.txt', 'w'). This creates a file object, erases any old marks.txt, and puts the pointer at 0.
f.write('Anil 78\n') writes 8 characters: A, n, i, l, space, 7, 8, newline. It returns 8. The pointer moves to 8.
f.write('Bina 91\n') writes 8 characters and returns 8. The pointer moves to 16.
f.close() flushes the buffer. The file now holds 16 characters.
Open in append mode: open('marks.txt', 'a'). f.write('Chetan 65\n') writes 10 characters and returns 10. The file now holds 26 characters.

Close, then open in read mode: open('marks.txt', 'r'). f.readline() returns 'Anil 78\n'. Because all these characters are ASCII, the pointer moves to position 8, so f.tell() returns 8. For non-ASCII text, treat the value from tell() as an opaque position and pass it back to seek(); do not count characters.
examples.answer: The writes return 8, 8 and 10 characters; the file holds 16 characters before the append and 26 after it; readline() returns 'Anil 78\n' and tell() reports 8 because the text is ASCII.

traps: Mode 'w' erases an existing file at open, before you write one character. A wrong mode loses the old data.
A file left open may never flush its buffer. Use close() or with, especially after writing.
read() at end of file returns an empty string '', not an error. A manual read loop must test for '' or use a for loop.
write() returns the number of characters written and adds no newline. Putting '\n' in the string is your job.
FileNotFoundError comes from open() in 'r' when the file is missing. Modes 'w' and 'a' create the file instead.

quiz.a: It opens data.txt for appending. Writes go to the end, and existing text is kept.

quiz.q: Why does f.write(78) fail while f.write(str(78)) works?
quiz.a: A text file stores characters, and write() needs a string. str(78) makes the string '78'. The integer 78 is not text.

quiz.q: For f = open('marks.txt', 'w'), what does n = f.write('Anil 78\n') return, and where is the pointer?
quiz.a: The string 'Anil 78\n' has 8 characters, so n is 8 and the pointer is at position 8.

quiz.q: A file starts with 'Anil 78\nBina 91\n'. After f.readline(), what does f.tell() return?
quiz.a: readline() consumes 'Anil 78\n'. For this ASCII text the pointer position is 8, so tell() returns 8. The value is an opaque position; with non-ASCII text it need not equal the character count.

quiz.q: Why can a second f.read() return '' even when the file has text?
quiz.a: The first read() moved the pointer to end of file. The second read() starts there, finds no characters, and returns ''.

quiz.q: Compare 'w' and 'a' for a file that already holds 100 characters.
quiz.a: 'w' erases the 100 characters at open and starts empty. 'a' keeps them and writes new text after them.

quiz.q: Why is strip() used before int() when reading a number from a line?
quiz.a: The line includes '\n'. strip() removes that newline and spaces, so int() receives only the digits and sign.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real programs use with open(...) as the normal form, because it closes files on every exit path. Large logs are read line by line with for loops instead of read(), which keeps memory flat. Data that grows into tables moves to CSV or databases, and structured settings often use JSON. Search Python pathlib read_text write_text, context manager, buffered I/O and file descriptor.
